etymology: From Latin mendax, false, lying. Webster 1828 gives the noun as falsehood, and notes that its proper signification is a disposition to lie, or habitual lying.
biblical_def: Mendacity is falsehood as a habit, not a slip of the tongue. Lying lips are abomination to the LORD, but they that deal truly are His delight (Pro 12:22). The new man is charged, Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds (Col 3:9). A single lie is sin. Mendacity is the settled disposition to lie, and the church is not permitted to baptize it as strategy.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MENDAC'ITY as falsehood, and notes that its proper signification is a disposition to lie, or habitual lying.
webster_full: MENDAC'ITY, noun [Latin mendax, false, lying.] Falsehood.
[The proper signification of this word would be a disposition to lie, or habitual lying.]
scriptures: Proverbs 12:22
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
Colossians 3:9
Lie not one to another, seeing that ye have put off the old man with his deeds;
corruption_summary: The age renames mendacity as narrative, branding, or a personal truth that need not match the fact.
corruption_paragraphs: A disposition to lie is now often praised when it serves a cause, a brand, or a man's image. Scripture does not grade the lie by its usefulness. Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD.
The other dodge is to call every sharp truth unkind, so that only the habitual liar sounds pastoral. Dealing truly is the delight of God. Habitual lying is not a communication style.
roots_summary: Latin mendax means false, lying. The KJV speaks of lying lips and of lying one to another. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin mendax — false, lying; a disposition to falsehood.
KJV lying lips are an abomination to the LORD (Pro 12:22).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun mendacity.
usage: Mendacity is habitual lying, not a clever narrative.
Lying lips are an abomination, not a tool of ministry.
Deal truly. The new man does not lie to his brother.

etymology: From Latin lassitudo, from lassus, weary, kin to laxus, slack. Webster 1828 names weakness, dullness, heaviness, and languor of body or mind from exhausted strength.
biblical_def: Lassitude is weariness that slackens the hand from the work God has given. Let us not be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not (Gal 6:9). They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall run, and not be weary, and they shall walk, and not faint (Isa 40:31). Bodily exhaustion is real. The sin is treating that heaviness as a discharge from well doing.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LAS'SITUDE as weakness, dullness, heaviness, and weariness; languor of body or mind from exhaustion of strength.
webster_full: LAS'SITUDE, noun [Latin lassitudo, from lassus, and this from laxus, laxo, to relax.]
1. Weakness; dullness; heaviness; weariness; languor of body or mind, proceeding from exhaustion of strength by excessive labor or action, or other means.
2. Among physicians, lassitude is a morbid sensation or languor which often precedes disease, in which case it proceeds from an impaired or diseased action of the organs.
scriptures: Galatians 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Isaiah 40:31
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
corruption_summary: Lassitude is now often crowned as burnout, a moral credential that excuses the neglect of duty.
corruption_paragraphs: Weariness of body is not a virtue, and it is not a license. The age tells a man that heaviness itself proves he has done enough, so the field may lie until he feels ready. Scripture says the opposite: do not be weary in well doing.
Webster already knew a morbid languor that precedes disease. That is a matter for rest and medicine. It is not the same thing as a slack soul that will not wait on the LORD for renewed strength.
roots_summary: Latin lassitudo is weariness, a slackening. The KJV speaks of being weary in well doing, and of walking and not fainting. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin lassus — weary; kin to slackness, a relaxed strength.
KJV weary in well doing is the danger named to the churches (Gal 6:9).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun lassitude.
usage: Lassitude is heaviness of body or mind, not a medal for quitting.
Do not faint in well doing. The harvest is in due season.
Wait on the LORD. He renews strength.

etymology: From Latin parsimonia, from parcus, sparing, close. Webster 1828 allows a cautious sense near frugality, but more generally an excessive closeness allied to covetousness, and a want of honorable liberality.
biblical_def: Parsimony is a closeness with money that withholds more than is meet. There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty (Pro 11:24). He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly, and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully (2Co 9:6). Frugality is not the sin. The sin is a sparingness that will not do the works of liberality.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines P'ARSIMONY as closeness or sparingness in expenditure; sometimes near frugality, but more generally an excessive closeness allied to covetousness, and a want of honorable liberality.
webster_full: P'ARSIMONY, noun [Latin parsimonia, from parcus, saving, literally close; Eng. park.] Closeness or sparingness in the use or expenditure of money; sometimes used perhaps in a good sense, implying due or justifiable caution in expenditure, in which sense it differs little from frugality and economy. More generally, it denotes an excessive caution or closeness; in which case, it is allied to covetousness, but it implies less meanness than niggardliness. It generally implies some want of honorable liberality.
The ways to enrich are many; parsimony is one of the best, and yet is not innocent, for it withholdeth men from works of liberality.
scriptures: Proverbs 11:24
There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty.
2 Corinthians 9:6
But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully.
corruption_summary: Parsimony is rebranded as financial wisdom, while real liberality is mocked as naive.
corruption_paragraphs: A man can call a locked purse prudence and still be withholding more than is meet. Webster already said this closeness is not innocent, because it withholds men from works of liberality. Proverbs says that withholding tends to poverty, not to safety.

The opposite corruption spends the household into ruin and calls the waste faith. Scripture does not baptize either error. Sow bountifully where God has commanded. Do not hoard under the name of caution.
roots_summary: Latin parsimonia is sparingness. The KJV speaks of withholding more than is meet, and of sowing sparingly. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin parcus — sparing, close in expenditure.
KJV withholdeth more than is meet tends to poverty (Pro 11:24).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun parsimony.
usage: Parsimony is excessive closeness, not honorable thrift.
Do not withhold more than is meet.
He who sows sparingly reaps sparingly.

etymology: Webster 1828 defines prodigality as extravagance in expenditure, particularly of money: profusion, waste, and excessive liberality, opposed to frugality and parsimony.
biblical_def: Prodigality is waste of what one possesses, spending as if the gift had no Giver. The younger son gathered all together, and wasted his substance with riotous living (Luk 15:13). He that loveth pleasure shall be a poor man: he that loveth wine and oil shall not be rich (Pro 21:17). There is a scattering that increases. This is not that. This is substance poured out on riot, until the man is empty.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PRODIGAL'ITY as extravagance in expenditure, particularly of money; profusion; waste; excessive liberality, opposed to frugality and parsimony.
webster_full: PRODIGAL'ITY, noun
1. Extravagance in the expenditure of what one possesses, particularly of money; profusion; waste; excessive liberality. It is opposed to frugality, economy, and parsimony.
By the Roman law a man of notorious prodigality was treated as non compos.
The most severe censor cannot but be pleased with the prodigality of his wit.
2. Profuse liberality.
scriptures: Luke 15:13
And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.
Proverbs 21:17
He that loveth pleasure shall be a poor man: he that loveth wine and oil shall not be rich.
corruption_summary: Prodigality is sold as generosity, lifestyle, or a man who knows how to live.
corruption_paragraphs: Waste of substance is not open-handedness. The prodigal son did not sow bountifully toward God or the poor. He wasted his substance with riotous living. The age still applauds that riot when the receipts look like hospitality.
Webster opposed prodigality to frugality, not to cruelty. A household can be ruined by profusion and still be told it was loving. Love does not devour the inheritance for pleasure.
roots_summary: The English noun names extravagance and waste. The KJV pictures a son who wasted his substance with riotous living. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Webster: extravagance, profusion, waste, excessive liberality.
KJV wasted his substance is the prodigal's road (Luk 15:13).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun prodigality.
usage: Prodigality is waste, not generosity.
Do not love pleasure until the house is poor.
Riotous living spends what God gave to be stewarded.

etymology: From Latin temeritas, properly a rushing forward. Webster 1828 defines it as rashness, an unreasonable contempt of danger, and extreme boldness.
biblical_def: Temerity is rashness that despises danger and will not wait on God. Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few (Ecc 5:2). A wise man feareth, and departeth from evil: but the fool rageth, and is confident (Pro 14:16). Courage counts the cost and obeys. Temerity rushes, and calls the rush faith.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TEMER'ITY as rashness; unreasonable contempt of danger; and extreme boldness.
webster_full: TEMER'ITY, noun [Latin temeritas; properly a rushing forward.]
1. Rashness; unreasonable contempt of danger; as the temerity of a commander in war.
2. Extreme boldness.
The figures are bold even to temerity
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 5:2
Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few.
Proverbs 14:16
A wise man feareth, and departeth from evil: but the fool rageth, and is confident.
corruption_summary: Temerity is marketed as bold leadership, disruption, and a confidence that will not count the cost.
corruption_paragraphs: A commander who holds danger in contempt is not thereby brave. Webster called that temerity. The fool in Proverbs rages and is confident. The wise man fears, and departs from evil.
The church is not helped by vows, campaigns, and public words poured out in haste before God. Few words are the command, because God is in heaven and the speaker is on earth.
roots_summary: Latin temeritas is a rushing forward. The KJV forbids a rash mouth and a hasty heart before God. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin temeritas — rashness; a rushing forward.
KJV be not rash with thy mouth (Ecc 5:2).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun temerity.
usage: Temerity is unreasonable contempt of danger, not courage.
Be not rash with your mouth before God.
The fool rages and is confident. The wise man fears.

etymology: From Latin ob and probrum, disgrace. Webster 1828 defines opprobrium as reproach mingled with contempt or disdain.
biblical_def: Opprobrium is reproach mingled with contempt. Because for thy sake I have borne reproach; shame hath covered my face (Psa 69:7). Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach (Heb 13:13). Christ pleased not Himself. The reproaches of them that reproached God fell on Him (Rom 15:3). To bear that reproach with Him is honor. To invent contempt for the righteous is sin.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OPPRO'BRIUM as reproach mingled with contempt or disdain.
webster_full: OPPRO'BRIUM, noun [Latin ob and probrum, disgrace.]
Reproach mingled with contempt or disdain.
scriptures: Psalm 69:7
Because for thy sake I have borne reproach; shame hath covered my face.
Hebrews 13:13
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
corruption_summary: The age treats all reproach as abuse to be escaped, and treats contempt of Christ's people as moral clarity.
corruption_paragraphs: Reproach for Christ's sake is not a brand injury to be managed away. Hebrews sends the church outside the camp to bear His reproach. Psalm 69 bears shame for God's sake and does not call it a mistake.
The other corruption heaps disdain on the godly and calls the heap honesty. Contempt is not discernment. Opprobrium invented against the righteous is the old scorn, not a new virtue.
roots_summary: Latin probrum is disgrace. The KJV speaks of bearing reproach for God's sake, and of going forth unto Christ bearing His reproach. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin ob and probrum — reproach, disgrace, disdain.
KJV bearing his reproach is the church's place outside the camp (Heb 13:13).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun opprobrium.
usage: Opprobrium is reproach mingled with contempt.
Bear Christ's reproach. Do not flee the camp to keep a reputation.
Do not invent disdain and call it honesty.

etymology: Webster 1828 defines peevishness as fretfulness, petulance, a disposition to murmur, and sourness of temper.
biblical_def: Peevishness is a sour temper that frets and murmurs instead of repenting. The foolishness of man perverteth his way, and his heart fretteth against the LORD (Pro 19:3). Do all things without murmurings and disputings (Php 2:14). Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil (Psa 37:8). A soft answer turns away wrath. A peevish heart stirs it, and then blames God for the tangle it made.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PEE'VISHNESS as fretfulness, petulance, a disposition to murmur, and sourness of temper.
webster_full: PEE'VISHNESS, noun Fretfulness; petulance; disposition to murmur; sourness of temper; as childish peevishness
When peevishness and spleen succeed.
scriptures: Proverbs 19:3
The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the LORD.
Philippians 2:14
Do all things without murmurings and disputings:
corruption_summary: Peevishness is recast as authenticity, a right to be sour, or a temperament no one may correct.
corruption_paragraphs: A disposition to murmur is not honesty about one's feelings. It is sourness of temper. Proverbs locates the fret in a heart that has already perverted its way, and then frets against the LORD.
The church is told to do all things without murmurings and disputings. Childish peevishness does not become mature because the man is older. It is still fretfulness, and it still stirs strife.
roots_summary: Webster names fretfulness and a disposition to murmur. The KJV forbids fretting against the LORD and murmuring in the work. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Webster: fretfulness, petulance, sourness of temper.
KJV his heart fretteth against the LORD (Pro 19:3).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun peevishness.
usage: Peevishness is sourness of temper, not candor.
Do not fret against the LORD for a way you perverted.
Do all things without murmurings and disputings.

etymology: From Latin imprudentia, want of prudence. Webster 1828 names indiscretion, want of caution and circumspection, heedlessness, and rashness as to the consequences of words and actions.
biblical_def: Imprudence is want of foresight, a refusal to regard the end of a word or a deed. A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished (Pro 22:3). He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly (Pro 14:29). The servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient (2Ti 2:24). Imprudence is not a charming simplicity. It is the simple passing on into punishment.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines IMPRU'DENCE as want of prudence; indiscretion; want of caution or circumspection; heedlessness; inconsiderateness; rashness.
webster_full: IMPRU'DENCE, noun [Latin imprudentia; in and prudentia, prudence.]

Want of prudence; indiscretion; want of caution, circumspection, or a due regard to the consequences of words to be uttered or actions to be performed, or their probable effects on the interest, safety, reputation or happiness of one's self or others; heedlessness; inconsiderateness; rashness. Let a man of sixty attempt to enumerate the evils which his imprudence has brought on himself, his family, or his neighbors.
scriptures: Proverbs 22:3
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.
Proverbs 14:29
He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.
corruption_summary: Imprudence is praised as spontaneity, authenticity, or a faith that will not look at consequences.
corruption_paragraphs: Want of caution is not spiritual freedom. Webster names the cost: words and actions whose probable effects on one's own house, and on a neighbor's, were never regarded. The simple pass on, and are punished.

A hasty spirit is not zeal. It exalts folly. The servant of the Lord is patient, because words have ends, and a man of years can count the evils his imprudence brought on his family and his neighbors.
roots_summary: Latin imprudentia is want of prudence. The KJV contrasts the prudent man who foresees evil with the simple who pass on. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin in and prudentia — want of foresight and caution.
KJV the simple pass on, and are punished (Pro 22:3).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun imprudence.
usage: Imprudence is heedlessness of consequences, not faith.
The prudent man foresees the evil and hides himself.
A hasty spirit exalts folly.
